rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's opponents had no proof, making themselves culpable; after doing nothing wrong, he had no reason to fear their objects of worship.
rows.anchor: then they are self-acknowledged criminals in the eyes of God. So, if he punishes them, they deserve it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓulm here means polytheism, as elsewhere in the Qur'an; acceptable faith must be entirely free of it.
rows.anchor: in the last verse refers to polytheism. It is used in this meaning at

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True security and guidance belong to people who trust God in all affairs and clear themselves of polytheism, rather than relying on deities.
rows.anchor: The fact is that peace is reserved for those who trust God in all affairs and absolve themselves of polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing statement refers to Abraham's conclusive monotheistic argument against his people, detailed in the preceding account.
rows.anchor: This is Our conclusive reasoning which We provided Abraham against his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author describes prophetic revelation as light upon light and refers readers to 24:35 for fuller discussion.
rows.anchor: darkness but of light upon light.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets begin by inviting their closest relatives; Abraham first invited his father before addressing his nation.
rows.anchor: He first invited his father and this precisely has been the way of prophets of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grand words Abraham utters in 6:79–80 are prophetic, confirming that the celestial argument occurred after his appointment.
rows.anchor: The grand words uttered in these verses by him can only be said by a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic revelation is described as light upon light, with fuller discussion under 24:35.
rows.anchor: darkness but of light upon light.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's argument from the celestial kingdom came after his appointment: prophets first invite their closest relatives, then address their nation, and 6:79–80 speaks with prophetic authority.
rows.anchor: The proof that this incident took place after Abraham (sws) was made a prophet is found in verses 79-80.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating the episode as an intellectual journey produces an illogical sequence: the small star appears first, while a cave story was invented to explain why Abraham saw Venus before the sun.
rows.anchor: A more illogical narrative had to be fabricated to justify this illogical sequence of observation:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual argument accepts an opponent's premise to trap him, not to endorse it; Abraham uses the celestial bodies' setting to defeat their claim that their shining proves divinity.
rows.anchor: if their shine is the proof of their divinity, then they should also witness their setting and fading away.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets use natural, context-sensitive methods including gradual reasoning, humor, sarcasm, and double meanings; an apparently affectionate pause or sarcasm can persuade beyond many arguments.
rows.anchor: These include gradual reasoning, humour, sarcasm, using words and sentences with double-meaning etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural, indefinite درجات is rendered 'ranks after ranks'; those who contemplate God's kingdom grow in knowledge, comprehension, faith, and rank, as 6:75 anticipates.
rows.anchor: those people who observe the kingdom of God, their knowledge, comprehension, faith and ranks are enhanced by Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's granting of higher ranks follows His knowledge and wisdom: He raises those who deserve it and fulfil His rights, rather than acting blindly.
rows.anchor: His desire is based on His knowledge and wisdom. He grants high status to those who deserve it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using one's intellect and innate capacities lifts celestial bodies above idols made by human hands; neglecting them leads to worshipping carved rocks.
rows.anchor: if a person does not use his intellect and innate abilities, he ends up prostrating before rocks he has carved out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's message achieves lasting worldly success through a progeny of prophets and righteous reformers, all preaching the monotheism also taught by Noah; if his people refuse, others will carry it.
rows.anchor: All of them preached the same religion of monotheism which he preached and which Noah before him preached.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite opposition, Abraham must follow the path of God's guided servants and tell his rivals he seeks no payment; the reminder benefits those who accept it, while rejecters face its consequences.
rows.anchor: Abraham (sws) must nevertheless follow the religion of those who were guided by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source says the Talmud records that Noah taught Abraham, implying that their generations were adjacent.
rows.anchor: It is known from the Talmud that Noah (sws) taught and instructed Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 'among his descendants,' the pronoun refers to Abraham.
rows.anchor: the antecedent of the pronoun is Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The listed figures are celebrated Israelite prophets; those in the first group share kingship or another leadership role.
rows.anchor: Also common to them is that all of them were either kings or held some or the other position of leadership.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Thus do We reward the righteous' explains their guidance as a reward for character and righteousness, not ancestry.
rows.anchor: this reward was not given to them because of their lineage but because of their attributes and character.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zacharias, John, Jesus, and Ilyas were guided to preach monotheism and Islam, were righteous rather than divine, and the two prophet groups contrast political leadership with asceticism.
rows.anchor: They also preached monotheism and Islam and not anything else.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilyas is Elijah of the Torah; the Qur'anic al-Yasa' is identified with Elisha rather than Isaiah, whose name is also similar.
rows.anchor: the pronunciation Elisha (sws) is closer to the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being exalted above the peoples refers to receiving the responsibility of preaching God's guidance.
rows.anchor: Exaltation here refers to the responsibility of preaching God’s guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's selection from among the prophets' forefathers, children, and siblings means choosing them to guide people and teach monotheism.
rows.anchor: is to select them for guiding people and teaching them monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The undefined expression for the straight path heightens its import and denotes the path of monotheism.
rows.anchor: refers to the path of monotheism and is undefined to enhance its import.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Chosen status is lost through polytheism and cannot rest on descent from Noah or Abraham; the warning addresses Arabs and Israelites, whose deeds then bear no fruit before God.
rows.anchor: Their chosen status merely because they were the descedents of Noah (sws) or Abraham (sws) will not remain intact.

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī distinguishes al-ḥukm from the more frequently paired al-ḥikmah and defines it as true understanding and deciding affairs by that understanding; when deeply rooted, it is ḥikmah.
rows.anchor:
ustādh Ḥamīd al-
Dīn Farāhī has said that it means “true understanding and to decide affairs in the light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book's ḥukm and ḥikmah guide both personal and collective life, including cases requiring inference; without this practical judgment scripture becomes merely historical.
rows.anchor: Both ḥukm and ḥikmah are essential consequences of being given the book of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave the earlier prophets scripture, judgment, and prophethood, and now intends these gifts to bless the people of Mecca through Muhammad; the Prophet should leave rejecting opponents to others entrusted with the mission.
rows.anchor: It is now through these gifts that the Almighty wants to bless the people of Makkah through prophet Muḥammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle ب indicates that making someone responsible also carries the sense of making them a guarantor.
rows.anchor: also encompasses the meaning “to make someone a guarantor.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The 'people' are the believing Companions and those destined to join them; their perseverance and the ummah's growth assure Muhammad that his preaching will succeed despite its small beginnings.
rows.anchor: These words predict the perseverance which will be shown by the companions and the abundance of the ummah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A waqfah mark after the clause about God's guidance means the Prophet should leave Satan-following claimants to Abraham's legacy to themselves; he preaches freely and God will reward him.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) should leave to themselves those who claim to be followers of Abraham (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun 'it' in 'a reminder for all people' refers to the Qur'an; once delivered, the Prophet has fulfilled his duty and need not force acceptance.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the pronoun “it” in “it is a mere reminder for all the people of the world” is the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an is a reminder of natural truths buried under desire and religious innovations, rather than something unknown or novel.
rows.anchor: The first of these is that whatever the Qur’ ān was presenting was not something unknown or unique

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder recalls the guidance of Noah, Abraham, and all prophets; later claimants distorted that legacy, while the Qur'an revives forgotten history and lessons of human nature.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān was reminding them of the very guidance which was brought forth by Noah (sws), Abraham (sws) and all prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section refutes religious innovations: crops and livestock are God's gifts to Quraysh, who should use them gratefully and fulfil their duties instead of imposing polytheistic rules, since Satan is their enemy.
rows.anchor: land-produce, cattle and live-stock are all created by God and it is because of His graciousness that the Quraysh are their beneficiaries.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The animal-prohibition challenge demands proof from Abraham's religion; without it, there is no basis for distinguishing permitted from forbidden offspring or fruit from one tree.
rows.anchor: when they cannot prove any of them to be prohibited, how can from among their offspring some be regarded as lawful and others unlawful?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation identifies the specific forbidden animals in Abraham's religion; Jewish prohibitions match these except restrictions imposed on them for rebellion.
rows.anchor: What was prohibited to the Jews was the same as prohibited in the religion of Abraham (sws) except the ones that were prohibited to them because of their rebelliousness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basic teachings of Abraham's religion call Quraysh to the straight path; Moses' law likewise guides its adherents to that path.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh too are invited to this straight path. They must not deviate from them and wander in misguidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealing the Qur'an to the Arabs is a great favour that conclusively conveys truth and leaves no excuse; waiting for punishment before believing will be futile.
rows.anchor: by revealing this Book the truth stands conclusively conveyed to them. They are now left with no excuse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet declares his whole life and worship devoted to God and invites others to Abraham's religion; each answers for their own deeds, while rebellious nations before Quraysh exemplify God's unchanged law.
rows.anchor: His prayer, his sacrifice, his life and death are all for God.

rows.claim: The rhetorical question asks on what basis the polytheists associated partners with God.
rows.anchor: The question implied is regarding the basis they have associated partners with God
